chunks: How a PLL works. The question: How does a PLL work?
A PLL is a feedback loop that makes an oscillator follow a reference clock.
It keeps checking whether the oscillator is early or late compared with the reference, and nudges it to fix the difference.
When the difference stops changing, the loop is "locked", and the output is an exact multiple of the reference.
Picture a cyclist trying to stay level with a friend. If the cyclist falls behind, pedal harder. If they pull ahead, ease off.
After a while they ride side by side at the same speed. The cyclist's pedaling effort is the control voltage.
The picture is loose in one way: the PLL compares when clock edges arrive, so it holds a timing gap steady, not a distance.
The classic charge-pump PLL. The closed path VCO to ÷N to PFD to charge pump to loop filter to VCO is a negative-feedback loop.
Locked, f fb equals f ref and so f out equals Nf ref .
Phase detector: compares edge timing of two clocks and outputs how early or late one is. Loop filter: smooths the detector's output into a steady control voltage.
VCO: an oscillator whose frequency depends on its control voltage. Lock: the state where the divided output matches the reference in frequency with a steady timing offset (phase).
Feedback divider: divides the output by N before comparing.
Reference is 25 megahertz and N equals 40 . Suppose the VCO starts at 900 megahertz. Divided by 40, that is 22. 5 megahertz, slower than the 25 megahertz reference.
The detector sees the feedback is late, the control voltage rises, and the VCO speeds up.
This continues until the VCO reaches 1 gigahertz, where the divided clock is exactly 25 megahertz and the correction stops. That is the whole idea.
"A PLL is a feedback loop that locks an oscillator's phase to a reference.
A phase-frequency detector compares the reference to the VCO output divided by N and generates pulses proportional to the phase error.
A charge pump and loop filter turn that into a control voltage, which steers the VCO.
When the divided clock has the same frequency as the reference and a constant phase offset, the control voltage stops changing: it's locked, and the output frequency is N times the reference.
The VCO's integration of frequency into phase is why the loop can lock with zero phase error."
